rows.answer: In a one-dimensional array, a peak is a local property [1]. An element is a peak if it is greater than or equal to the elements to its left and right [1]; for example, position 2 is a peak if and only if $b \ge a$ and $b \ge c$ [1][5]. For elements on the edges of the array, they only need to be greater than or equal to their single neighbor [3]; for instance, position 9 is a peak if $i \ge h$ [3][5].

In the case where the definition of a peak uses "greater than or equal to," any array will always have a peak [1]. However, if the definition is changed to "greater than," this argument cannot be made [1].

The straightforward peak finding algorithm starts from the left and walks across the array [2][3]. In the worst case, this algorithm has a complexity of $\Theta(n)$ [6], which is described as linear asymptotic complexity that requires a constant times $n$ [1].

The divide and conquer algorithm finds a peak in a 1D array using the following process [5]:

*   If $a[n/2] < a[n/2 - 1]$, the algorithm only looks at the left half (from $1 \dots n/2 - 1$) to look for a peak [5].
*   Else if $a[n/2] < a[n/2 + 1]$, the algorithm only looks at the right half (from $n/2 + 1 \dots n$) to look for a peak [5].
*   Otherwise, the $n/2$ position is a peak [5].

The complexity of this algorithm is $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1) = \Theta(\log_2(n))$ [5].

The time complexity of the 1D divide and conquer peak finder is $\Theta(\log_2(n))$ [1]. This is derived from the recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$, which results in $\Theta(1)$ being summed $\log_2(n)$ times [1]. This is also referred to as "log n complexity" [2][3].

An element $a$ is a 2D-peak if and only if $a \ge b, a \ge d, a \ge c, a \ge e$ [6]. In terms of array positions, an element $(i, j)$ is a 2D peak if it is greater than or equal to its neighbors to the left $(i, j-1)$ and right $(i, j+1)$, provided it is also the maximum element in its column, meaning it has been compared to all adjacent elements looking up and down [2].
The greedy ascent algorithm for 2D peak finding has a complexity of $\Theta(nm)$ [1][2][3]. In cases where $m = n$, the complexity is $\Theta(n^2)$ [1][2][3].

Finding a 1D peak in the middle column does not guarantee a 2D peak because, as seen in "Attempt #1" of the 2D peak finding problem, a 2D peak may not exist on the row $i$ where the 1D peak was found [3]. Consequently, this algorithm is incorrect [6].

The running time for the 2D peak algorithm that picks the middle column and finds its global maximum (referred to as Attempt #2) is $\Theta(n \log m)$, where $n$ is the number of rows and $m$ is the number of columns [3]. If $m = n$, the complexity is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [3].

This complexity is derived from the recurrence relation $T(n, m) = T(n, m/2) + \Theta(n)$, where $\Theta(n)$ is the work required to find the global maximum on a column [3].

The word "algorithm" comes from Al-Kharazmi [3], also spelled Al-Khwārizmī (c. 780-850) [4]. He is known as the "father of algebra" and wrote "The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing" [3][4]. This book focused on solving quadratic and linear equations, which are considered some of the first algorithms [3][4]. The word "algebra" shares the same roots as the word "algorithm" [1].

The Random Access Machine (RAM) is a theoretical model of computation [2][3][5]. It models Random Access Memory as a big array [3][4] organized by machine words, consisting of $\Theta(1)$ registers where each register is 1 word [3][4].

Key characteristics of the RAM model include:
*   **Structure and Access:** The model consists of cells indexed starting from $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...$ [1]. If the location of an element is known, any part of the array can be accessed in constant time [4].
*   **Design:** It is designed to be super simple to ensure that operations take constant time [5]. While it is a powerful and realistic model, it does not feature dynamic memory allocation [6].
*   **Technical Specifications:** The model uses mathematical notations including operations such as $(+, -, *, /, \&, |, \wedge)$ and a word size $w \ge \lg(\text{memory size})$ bits [1].

A pointer machine is a model of computation that corresponds to a simple version of object-oriented programming [1]. Its key characteristics include:

*   **Objects:** It uses dynamically allocated objects [1][5]. Each object must have a constant number of fields, or $O(1)$ fields [1][2][5].
*   **Fields:** A field can be either a word—such as an integer, a counter, or a computed value—or a pointer (also known as a reference) [1][5]. A pointer points to another object or has a special value of null, nil, or none [1][5].
*   **Operations and Constraints:** Manipulating an object with a constant number of attributes takes constant time [2]. The model supports dynamic memory allocation through the creation and destruction of nodes [4]. Unlike pointers in C, pointers in this model cannot be "touched" (for example, one cannot add one to a pointer to move to the next item) [4].
*   **Relationship to RAM:** The pointer machine is weaker than the Random Access Memory (RAM) model and can be implemented on a RAM by treating a pointer as an index into a giant table [4][5].

An example of a pointer machine structure is a doubly linked list, where each node contains a value and pointers to the next and previous elements [3][4].

Appending an item to a Python list takes $\theta(1)$ time [4][6], which is constant time [2]. While allocating a new array and copying all elements would take linear time, Python does not use that method [1]; instead, it achieves $\theta(1)$ time via table doubling [4].

To define the distance between two documents, a document $D$ is first treated as a vector where $D[w]$ represents the number of occurrences of a word $W$ in that document [2][3]. In this context, a word is a sequence of alphanumeric characters and a document is a sequence of words [3].

The distance is defined as the angle between these two vectors [1][4]. This is expressed as $d(D_1, D_2) = \arccos(d//(D_1, D_2))$ [1]. An angle of $0^\circ$ indicates that the two documents are identical, while an angle of $90^\circ$ indicates that they share no common words [1][4]. This approach uses normalization by the number of words to ensure the measure is scale invariant, which prevents long documents with 99% of the same words from appearing farther apart than short documents with only 10% of the same words [1][3].

Insertion sort works by iterating through an input array and inserting each element into its correct position [1]. For $i = 1, 2, \dots, n$, the algorithm assumes that the elements from $a[0]$ through $a[i-1]$ are already sorted and then inserts $a[i]$ into the correct position [1].

This process is carried out using pairwise swaps [1][4]. Specifically, an element at index $j$ is designated as the "key" and is moved to a new location at index $i$ through a series of pairwise key-swaps [6]. For example, if the key is 3, it would be swapped with elements such as 6, 5, and 4 until it is greater than the preceding element, such as 2 [4].

Insertion sort is an in-place sorting algorithm with $\Theta(1)$ constant auxiliary space, as it only requires a temporary variable to store a value when swapping two elements [2].

Using binary search in insertion sort does not result in an overall $\Theta(n \log n)$ running time because, while binary search reduces the time to find the correct insertion position to $\Theta(\log n)$ [1][6], the elements in an array structure must still be shifted to the right to make room for the insertion [2][3]. This shifting process takes $\Theta(n)$ time [1][6]. Consequently, while the number of comparisons is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [1][2][3][6], the complexity for swaps remains $\Theta(n^2)$ [2][4][6].

The merge step in merge sort uses a "merge routine" [2] or "two-finger algorithm" [6] to combine two sorted arrays into a single sorted array by interleaving or interspersing the elements [6].

The process works as follows:
*   The algorithm uses pointers to "walk up" the two sorted arrays [3].
*   The smallest available elements from each array are compared, and the smaller of the two is selected to be placed next in the merged sequence [1].
*   This process is repeated until the arrays are combined into a sorted array [3].
*   In the broader context of merge sort, this routine begins at the leaves by merging pairs of elements, then merges those results into larger tuples (such as merging two pairs to get four elements) as it moves up [5].

The time complexity to merge a total of $n$ elements is $\Theta(n)$ [1][4][6].
Merge sort requires $\Theta(n)$ auxiliary space [2]. This extra memory is needed to perform the recursion and then place the results into the sorted array A [2].

The running time of merge sort is $\Theta(n \log n)$ [3][6].

This can be seen through the following methods:
*   **Recurrence Relation:** The time complexity $T(n)$ can be expressed as a recurrence where $T(n) = \Theta(1)$ if $n = 1$, and $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ if $n > 1$ [2]. This is also written as $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn$, where $c > 0$ is a constant [6].
*   **Recursion Tree:** Using a recursion tree, it can be seen that there is an equal amount of work done at each level, leading to a total complexity of $\Theta(n \lg n)$ [6].
*   **Other Methods:** Intuition can be gained through a "proof by picture" [3], and the recurrence can be solved using substitution [3].
